embedded_texts: How much weight should a late start on a deadline task carry when the same writer clearly did other parts of the work well ahead of time?
When someone's own time estimate for a job is exceeded, how do I separate a genuine estimation problem from an ordinary overrun?
What does it tell me when a writer's estimate turned out accurate for work they know well?
How can I check whether broken sleep is a better explanation than an attentional trait for delays in getting started?
A person with no real difficulties writes a very thorough logistical message; what should I take from the amount of arranging it shows?
Is a small line about buying something that may already be owned worth reading as a sign of not checking or forgetting?
What does a quick switch to a backup plan when the first option falls through suggest about organisation?
Should informal features such as missing capitals or no greeting be counted as evidence in a short family message?
How do I read drifting onto side jobs during a dull task when the person has recently suffered a loss?
Do self-built routines such as timed work blocks or a planner count for or against attentional difficulty, and what can the text not say about them?
What does it mean when a short errand repeatedly ends somewhere unrelated and the original item is not completed?
If someone can concentrate for a long stretch in a suitable place, does that argue against an attention problem?
How should I interpret evidence that a person reliably delivers work when somebody external is waiting for it?
How do caffeine and pre-exam nerves change the way I read restlessness and wandering in a text?
Which extra writing samples or background details should I ask for before a single entry can mean anything?
How do I tell worry that circles one theme from a wandering of attention away from the point?
A writer interrupts their own account with a tangent and then apologises; how much does this self-correction matter?
When a task goes wrong in a work handover, how do I decide whether the cause lies with the person or with circumstances?
What should I make of paperwork that is repeatedly promised and still left undone, especially when there is a real cost?
How far can long working hours and tiredness account for postponed administrative tasks?
In a polite, apologetic message asking for help, how do I separate anxiety about asking from attentional problems?
How should a very recent big life change shape how I read lapses reported in a help-seeking message?
How much does walking into a room and forgetting why you went in count as evidence of memory problems?
What does a gap between knowing exactly what to do and actually doing it suggest, and what else could produce it?
Can flawless performance in an emergency rule out attentional lapses seen elsewhere in the same writer's day?
What is the value of a note-to-self workaround for misplaced lists, and what could the habit mean?
How do I handle typing errors and clipped style in a message written on a phone at the end of a long shift?
When someone acts sharply in anger, how do I decide between impulsivity as a trait and a short fuse from low mood?
What does a writer's recognition of their own contribution to a conflict tell me?
If the rest of the day shows precise, planned and finished work, how much should one emotional flare count?
How much weight can retold family stories about someone's early years carry when the person does not recall them?
Why might repeated comments from schoolteachers be more useful than anecdotes, and what else could explain them?
What childhood records or questions would help me settle whether difficulties began early?
How should I interpret a person who does well when expectations are clear or the task interests them?
Is a long, chatty and digressive written account a sign of disorganised thinking, or just a style?
How should I treat a secondhand report that someone talked non-stop and barely remembers it?
A brief, self-noticed stall before starting a chore in an otherwise orderly entry: is it worth following up?
How do I read schedule overruns in the daily routine of a parent of small children?
What are the typical ways a less experienced reader over-reads ordinary stress as an attention problem in a text that is mostly organised?
If a day ended with everyone arriving on time despite delays, should punctuality count as evidence against difficulty?

Thursday night and the quarterly report is due tomorrow at five, which is fine, because the numbers from claims came in on Tuesday and I had already pulled the loss ratios into the template by Wednesday lunch, and then Priya asked me to check her reserve figures too, and that took the whole afternoon, and the lift in our building was out so I carried the shopping up four floors, which has nothing to do with anything but my legs hurt. Anyway the report.
I told myself two hours for the commentary section and it has now been most of the evening, I only opened the document at nine because I did the dishes and the bins first.

Still sleeping badly since we moved flats two months ago, the street is louder than the old one and the bed is a different bed, so I was up at five anyway and sent the chart pack to Marcus before work, and he replied with a thumbs up by eight.
That part went well.
The commentary I think I can finish by eleven, maybe midnight, then read through it once in the morning.
Need to remember to ask Dan about the fridge shelf.
Chapter three is at 1,100 words.
It goes to my supervisor on the 20th and today is the 11th.
I would call this a tragedy but it is mostly arithmetic.
On Monday I wrote 600 of those words in one go at the library, because the kitchen at home was empty and nobody was cooking. That went fine.
On Tuesday I opened the file, went to find the table from the second survey, and came back ten minutes later with a clean mug and no table.
I have had four coffees today. I know.
The stats exam is on Thursday as well and I am quite nervous about it.
I did send the method section on time last week, so at least one person at the university has proof I exist.
My supervisor wrote back with three comments, all fair, and I fixed them the same evening.
Today I made a plan of two blocks of 50 minutes with my phone in my bag. Block one happened.
Then I went to the kitchen to ask my flatmate about the bins and came back with a toastie and still no answer about the bins.
Block two is after dinner.
Hi Jo, you asked how the handover went and I said fine, which was not true.
Here is what happened.
Dana moved to the events team on Friday, so on Thursday I was meant to take over her campaign calendar and the supplier logins.
The logins worked, because I asked IT on Monday and they sorted it the same day.
The calendar did not, because she'd saved it as a local file and nobody told me, so for two days I was working from the old shared version.
That's the ordinary reason, really.
Anyway, my sister has the same problem with her boiler manual, it's a PDF on a laptop she has since sold, and her whole building spent a weekend... sorry.
The newsletter went out on Tuesday with the wrong date for the webinar.
I'd allowed an hour to check the proofs and it took nearer three, so the last two pages got a quick look.
Priya in design also copied me on a message that I keep going over in my head, the one about 'ownership', but that's another email.
So it was a local file, a wrong date and rushed proofing.
I'm sorry this ran so long.
Same story every month and I'm fed up with it.
A job I quote at about two days ends up three.

Last week it was a rewire in a 1960s semi, I said about two and a half days and it took four, though a fair bit of that was the plaster being thicker than it looked and the old cable run under the floor not where the drawings said.
That's the house, not me.
The week before I did a consumer unit swap in one morning, exactly as quoted, customer was pleased and paid by card on the spot.
So I can do it when I know the job.
Business has got busier since spring, I'm on site by seven most days and not home till gone seven, and by then I'm shattered. Invoices wait.
I'll do them soon, usually Sunday.
Right now there are six sitting in a folder, the oldest about five weeks, and I keep saying I'll sit down with them after tea.
One of them I did start, got as far as the customer's address.
Anyone else use an app on the phone for this?
Might try one soon.
Hello, I'm very sorry to trouble you, and I hope this is the right way to ask for an appointment.
I'm 27 and have been registered with you since university, though I've only been in twice.
Three weeks ago I started my first job, at a logistics firm, and honestly I think some of this is just that it's new and I'm trying hard not to get things wrong.
The first week was fine.
I was early every day and finished my induction modules by the Friday, which I was pleased about.
Since then a few things have slipped.
Last Tuesday my manager asked me to send a supplier a corrected spreadsheet, and I knew exactly what to do, but it sat open on my screen until the next afternoon before I sent it.
Twice I've walked into the stock room and forgotten what I went in for, which I know is small.
My manager has been kind about it, and the planner I bought last week has helped with remembering meetings.
I'm sorry this is so long.
Could I please have an appointment, either early morning or after 5pm, as I would rather not explain to work yet?
Wed. 6:50, bus in ten. Week so far.
Mon was quiet apart from bed 14 who coded at 3, we got him back, handover done by 7 with nothing missed.
Tue the pharmcy delivery came late so I spent an hour chasing saline stock, not my fault for once.
Went to do the fluid balance on bed 9 and ended up restocking glove boxes down the whole corridor, remembered the chart at 5. Done before handover anyway.
Last night Dana covered my break and I sat down for the full 30 min, ate the rice thing. Nothing happened.
Need to ask about swapping the Sunday, wrote it on my hand because the list is in my locker. or my coat.
Typing this on my phone with useless thumbs after twelve hours so excuse the typos. Bus. Also milk.
So I was going through the box Mum sent and found my year four report.
Mrs Okafor wrote that I was capable, polite and a strong reader, which is nice to see in her handwriting.
Mum says I would sit at the kitchen table with the maths sheet for most of the evening, pencil sharpened twice, before I wrote a single number.
I don't actually remember that, it's one of her stories, same as the one about me walking home the long way and arriving an hour late because I was watching the men dig up the road.
Dad tells that one every Christmas.
What I do remember myself is the science fair, year six or seven, I'm hazy.
I planned the volcano the week before, bought the baking soda on the Tuesday and had it finished early.
It got a ribbon.
Mr Doyle wrote that I was a pleasure to teach when I knew what was expected.
The handwriting comment came every year though, untidy and rushed.
You got the neat ones.
I'd love to see yours if Mum kept them, she said the loft, or maybe the garage.
Tuesday. The lunch boxes were packed yesterday evening, so that part cost nothing.
Oskar ate his porridge without any complaint.
Lena wanted the blue cup and I gave her the blue cup.
That was a calm ten minutes.
I had told myself shoes and coats would take five minutes. It took twenty.
Lena's left boot had gone missing.
We found it under the radiator in the hall.
Her coat zip also jammed halfway up, and I had to take it off her and start again.
After that I stood at the kitchen counter looking at the school bags and did not start on them for a while.
I am not sure what I was waiting for.
Then I put the reading folders in and zipped them.
The baby was up three times in the night.
Oskar remembered his swimming kit without being asked.
I think swimming is on Thursday, though.
We left the house at 8:25, ten minutes later than I wanted.
The walk to school takes fifteen minutes and we reached the gate at 8:40.
That was five minutes before the bell.
The teacher at the gate said hello to both of them.
Back home I put the dishes in the machine and wiped the table.
